articles.title: ‘I just want to go home.’ Passengers stranded at Logan Airport amid nationwide ground stop
articles.text:
‘I just want to go home.’ Passengers stranded at Logan Airport amid nationwide ground stop | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The flight status board at Boston's Logan Airport Friday during a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel from coast to coast. (Eve Zuckoff/WBUR)
Peter and Maria Silletti’s daughter is a college cheerleader in North Carolina. She’s a senior, and her final game begins early Saturday morning.
But Friday night, the proud North Andover parents found themselves stranded at Boston’s Logan Airport, caught in a nationwide ground stop that abruptly froze air travel and upended plans from coast to coast.
So instead the Sillettis were about to walk a mile to a car rental agency and then embark on a 12-hour drive to make it to their daughter’s game.
"We're going to go overnight,” Peter Silletti said. “We've done it before. So it's okay. We're not going to miss this.”
Outside the security gates, would-be passengers were glued to their phones and laptops. Some, like the Sillettis, scrambled to book rental cars before they ran out, others called their loved ones to rearrange plans, a few joked about it being Friday the 13th. The departures board showed a handful of cancellations, but most flights were listed as delayed.
Nick Benton was going home to Florida to bury his grandfather. Benton’s flight hadn’t been canceled yet, but he wasn’t optimistic he’d make it to the funeral Saturday.
“He was 93. He lived a damn good life,” Benton said. “This is kind of a little disappointing if it doesn't happen. But if it doesn't happen, there's not much I can really do about it.”
Massport, which operates Logan, told passengers to check with their airlines for flight updates. Gov. Maura Healey posted a statement on social media saying she’d been briefed on the ground stop and was “working to get answers from federal officials.”
Erica Ambrose had been trying to get home to New York from Atlanta since Thursday. Her first flight was delayed, then canceled, she said. Her next flight was also canceled. She expected the same thing to happen to her current flight.
“Even if it’s not, I don’t know if I’d actually feel comfortable flying,” Ambrose said with a laugh. At this point, she'd feel more comfortable driving.
“I’m tired,” Ambrose said. “I just want to go home.”

articles.title: Flights halted at airports across U.S. due to air traffic control communications problems
articles.text:
Flights halted at airports across U.S. due to air traffic control communications problems | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A Delta Airlines and United Airlines plane are seen at Denver International Airport on Nov. 6, 2026. (David Zalubowski/AP file)
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating.
On social media, Boston's Logan International Airport said they are "monitoring the situation" and passengers should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates.
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage."
“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” Mullin said.
There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.
But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
With additional reporting by WBUR's Dan Guzman

articles.title: The race is on: Boston City Council candidate launches challenge to Ed Flynn, Wu’s biggest critic
articles.text:
The race is on: Boston City Council candidate launches challenge to Ed Flynn, Wu’s biggest critic | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn spoke during an event in September 2021. (Jesse Costa/WBUR file)
Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn officially has some competition for his seat. He’ll face Rachael Pearson, a South Boston substitute teacher and community organizer, in the race to represent a district that includes South Boston, Chinatown and parts of the South End.
Kicking off what could be a competitive, high-dollar race in the city’s 2027 election cycle, Pearson welcomed supporters to a campaign launch at a Southie bar on Thursday night, where she told a crowd of around 150 people she’s focused on collaboration, advocacy and service.
“Let’s build a campaign that respects and reflects District 2,” told the room. “I may not have all of the answers, but I promise to be present.”
Pearson moved to Boston more than 22 years ago. She’s since spent her time leading the nonprofit South Boston Moms Club, a parental support group, raising funding for cancer research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute/The Jimmy Fund and filling in as a substitute teacher at the Oliver Hazard Perry School, which teaches students from kindergarten through sixth grade.
Pearson didn’t mention Flynn at her launch, and the eight-year incumbent from South Boston declined to comment on her announcement.
Flynn, a Navy veteran, former probation officer, youth sports coach and son of a former Boston mayor, has amassed nearly $1 million in campaign funds, an unusually large sum for a city councilor. Every other member of the 13-member body is currently reporting less than $75,000.
For years, the District 2 incumbent has been one of the most vocal critics of Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, criticizing many of her administration’s policies, from safety to spending matters. Some view his role on the council as a counterweight; others, a nuisance.
According to campaign finance records, Pearson has contributed $1,050 to the mayor’s past campaigns — and a total of $1,100 more to City Councilors Ruthzee Louijuene and Sharon Durkan.
Wu was not at Pearson's campaign launch, but a spokesperson for the mayor said she "is always thrilled when great people step forward to serve their communities."
Pearson could potentially benefit from Wu’s support. This fall, Wu backed two state Senate candidates who ran competitive — though ultimately unsuccessful — campaigns against incumbents after she fought with the longtime lawmakers over shifting the city’s property tax burden from homeowners to commercial business owners.
There may be more members of the Council-curious-class announcing runs in the near future.
With annual fundraising caps from individual donors that reset in January, some may choose to go public with their campaigns — or at least fundraise for them — before the calendar year ends so they can get a second bite at the apple from the same donors in 2027. The cap per year is $1,000.
This article was originally published on November 13, 2026.

articles.title: Nervous about baking pie this Thanksgiving? Here are tips from Boston’s preeminent pie makers
articles.text:
Nervous about baking pie this Thanksgiving? Here are tips from Boston’s preeminent pie makers | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Pumpkin pie at Flour Bakery. (Courtesy Flour Bakery)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox,  sign up here.
Thanksgiving is less than two weeks away so perhaps you've begun to plan what’s going to be on your table. You can’t go wrong with the classics: turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, etc.
And then, of course, there's the pie.
But if you, like me, have been watching a lot of “The Great British Bake Off” lately, you're ready to go beyond the store-bought pies. Put on an apron. Make your own showstopper. Get a handshake from Paul Hollywood (or more likely, your mom) for a pie well baked.
Then, you look up a recipe and suddenly you’re overwhelmed with questions. Should I pre-bake my pie shell? How much filling is too much? How do I avoid a soggy bottom? How do I know when my pie is cooked and ready?
Fret not! Your bake-off dream is still in sight! WBUR chatted with some expert local bakers to get their tips and tricks, and our roster is deep. (Even experienced pie-makers may have something to learn from these pros.)
Joanne Chang, owner of Boston-based Flour Bakery
Fran Kolenik, owner of Drive-By-Pies in Brookline
Jill Remby, owner of Petsi Pies in Somerville
Lauren Sherlock, owner of Big Little Pies in Boston
Thiago Silva, chef and owner of Salt Patisserie in Newton
Andrea DiReda Taber, owner of Ever So Humble Pie Company in East Walpole
And trust us, they know Thanksgiving pies. Chang said Thanksgiving is Flour’s “Super Bowl” and expects to sell over 5,000 pies throughout November. Remby at Petsi Pies said the shop averages “a couple hundred pies” a week, but for Thanksgiving those sales turn up to 4,000 pies in four days. And Sherlock expects to make as many as 6,000 mini pies and 300 large pies this month.
Here are their recommendations to make your Thanksgiving guests take Nigella Lawson-sized bites of your picture perfect pastry. (Responses have been edited lightly for clarity and length.)
Blackberry mini pie from Big Little Pies. (Courtesy Gene Buonaccorsi)
What is your best pie baking advice?
Silva: “If you’re baking at home, desserts and pies are something you can get ahead on. Whenever you do Thanksgiving cooking, it’s a lot. You cook a lot of things and a lot of the food that you make has to be within the day of Thanksgiving.
“But pies, you should be making your shells right now. You can put those pie shells in the freezer right now so you’re not stressing that week of Thanksgiving  where you're running around trying to figure things out.”
Kolenik: “It’s all about temperature, especially pumpkin and pecan pies, the temperature is super important. Pumpkin pie has to be 175 to 180 degrees [Fahrenheit]. Once it is, you take it out. Even if it looks a little jiggly, it’s still done because it’s going to continue to cook when it comes out of the oven.”
DiReda Taber: “If anybody’s reading a cookbook on how to make a pie, there’s no secret why nobody wants to do it. Because when [the cookbooks] talk about pie crust, it sounds like you need a PhD in order to get it to come out right. They’ll tell you to make the butter into pea-shaped pieces, use ice water and don't overhandle the dough. They put the fear of God into you. So, I would say to people, just relax. The most important thing is don’t overhandle the dough.”
Sherlock: “If you’re slicing into it, don’t be impatient. Wait for the [pie] to cool. Otherwise it’s just going to be one gooey mess.”
Any mistakes you made baking pies that you’d want people to avoid making?
Chang: “I did not blind bake my pie crusts. Blind baking is when you bake the pie crust before adding any filling. If you pour filling into an unbaked pie tin the crust doesn't ever really fully bake and it gets soggy. Blind baking gives you the best possible flakiness and baked caramelization in your crust.”
Cranberry pear crostata pie at Flour Bakery. (Courtesy Flour Bakery)
Silva: “The worst outcome for me is to have a soggy bottom. You might have the most delicious filling, but if you have a soggy bottom and you look at that raw dough underneath that beautiful filling, to me that’s just so disappointing.
The biggest advice is blind baking. All you want to do is take your pie shell, put a piece of parchment paper over it, line it with weights and blind bake until it’s just yellowish and crisp all the way through. Blind baking is so essential to having a really good flaky crust.”
DiReda Taber: “Some of our best recipes were because somebody screwed up. Our signature pie is jumble berry: strawberries, blueberries and cranberries.
“One day, one guy was measuring out the strawberries and blueberries. When he put the strawberries in and went to get the blueberries, the other guy dumped in a bunch of rhubarb, thinking it was going to be a strawberry rhubarb pie. So instead of being strawberries, blueberries and cranberries for our jumbleberry pie, they made strawberries, blueberries and rhubarb.
“And I said let’s bake one and see how it is. So we did, we baked it up and it was an ‘Oh my God’ moment. And that pie became the summer medley, the sister pie to jumbleberry.”
What’s something you do that’s unconventional or untraditional?
Remby: “What makes dough this really beautiful and flaky [thing] you want in a pastry, and yet still can handle being thrown around? Eggs. Our pie dough has tons of eggs in it. [It] lets it still be tender but have the elasticity and the shelf life that we need.”
Silva: “With the pecan pie, the unconventional thing I do is having a French recipe as a layer between your flaky crust and your liquid pecan filling.  I add a hazelnut financier cake in between. So what that does is it prevents any of that moisture [from making your pie soggy] because if you make a pecan pie filling, it's usually a pretty loose fi

articles.title: Springfield City Council to consider full ban on cryptocurrency kiosks to prevent scams
articles.text:
Springfield City Council to consider full ban on cryptocurrency kiosks to prevent scams | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A Coinmover machine at Richdale food shop in Cambridge, where you can buy Bitcoin with cash. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
Springfield city councilors will consider eliminating cryptocurrency kiosks after police and city officials say residents were scammed out of nearly $1 million.
The kiosks, also known as Bitcoin ATMs, look like most other ATMs and are often found in places like convenience stores or liquor stores. The kiosks allow people to purchase, sell or transfer virtual currency like Bitcoin.
Springfield Mayor Domenic Sarno introduced the proposed ordinance this week, arguing crypto kiosks have targeted "innocent people, especially our senior citizens."
"In just over a year, fraudsters and scammers who utilize these machines to target victims have scammed many hardworking and vulnerable people right here in Springfield out of nearly $1 million," Sarno said in a statement.
The proposed ban would require the kiosks be removed within 15 days the ordinance passes.
The Springfield Police Department said they've investigated nearly 50 cases in which residents or visitors were defrauded out of $968,528 between January 2025 and July 2026.
According to FBI data, Massachusetts saw 296 complaints about scams involving these types of ATMs last year — with nearly $7 million reported in losses.
Springfield police officials said the most common scheme involved scam callers pretending to be law enforcement, and that the fraudsters "use fear and urgency" to get victims to believe they need to pay a fine immediately.
"Once again, no police department. Sheriff’s department, or government agency will call asking for money in this manner," Springfield Police Superintendent Larry Akers said. "We have seen people scammed out of their [life] savings, and it is hard to trace and follow once it enters these machines.”
The Springfield City Council will vote on the proposed ordinance in December.
If passed, the city will join a handful of other Massachusetts communities that have banned Bitcoin ATMs, including Gloucester, Framingham, Ludlow and Haverhill.

articles.title: Republicans score rare blue-to-red flip in Maine during midterm landslide
articles.text:
Republicans score rare blue-to-red flip in Maine during midterm landslide | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, a candidate for Maine's second congressional House district, greets supporters, Aug. 24, 2026, in Brewer, Maine. (Gabe Souza/AP, File)
As Republicans dig out from under a midterm landslide, they can point to a single bright spot on the nationwide congressional map. That’s Maine’s 2nd congressional district, the only seat that went from blue to red without the help of redistricting.
It was far from a resounding victory. Even though President Donald Trump won the district by 9 points two years ago, it took a former Republican governor, Paul LePage, to squeak out a victory over Matt Dunlap, the Democratic state auditor.
The Associated Press called the race Thursday after officials finished the ranked choice voting process to determine the winner.
LePage and Dunlap were competing to replace Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat who is retiring from Congress.
The only other seats that went from blue to red are Texas' 32nd congressional district and Tennessee' 9th congressional district, but both of those flips were enabled by redistricting efforts that made the electorates far more conservative.
Meanwhile, Democrats have flipped 44 seats, and a handful of races have not yet been called.
Dunlap conceded last week and LePage declared victory, and he’s been in Washington for orientation for new members.
“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine,” said Brent Littlefield, a spokesperson for LePage.
Maine only has two congressional districts. The 1st is heavily Democratic and includes Portland and wealthy coastal towns. The 2nd includes a few small cities and vast rural and forested areas, and is home to industries such as logging, potato farming and lobster fishing. It’s more conservative than most of New England.
Golden had found success in the 2nd by running as a moderate Democrat who was willing to break with his party. However, he announced last year that he would not run for a fifth term, saying he had “grown tired of the increasing incivility and plain nastiness that are now common from some elements of our American community.”
As governor from 2010 to 2018, most of LePage’s two terms predated Trump’s presidency, but he aligned himself with the president toward the end of his time in office. The two shared a brand of brash, conservative populism, with LePage once saying he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular.”
However, LePage also criticized Trump's tariffs on Canada, a key trading partner for Maine, and expressed support for legal immigration. When he declared victory last week, LePage vowed to make the state’s interests a priority in Washington.
“If it is good for Maine, I will work hard to make it happen. If it is bad for Maine, I will oppose it,” he said.

Skip to main content

Phil Eng arrived in Boston in 2023, heralded as the savior of the run-down MBTA. Since then, the T's general manager preached a gospel of patience.
Eng has demonstrated an unprecedented willingness to shut down train lines and disrupt commutes in pursuit of ambitious repairs.
Former Massachusetts Assistant Secretary of Transportation Chris Dempsey and Boston Globe transportation reporter Diti Kohli join WBUR's Morning Edition to discuss how much longer T riders will be willing to endure the disruptions, and whether it will all be worth it.

articles.title: Mass. lawmakers plan to introduce 'Louisa's Law,' a street safety bill in the wake of Boston cyclist's death
articles.text:
Mass. lawmakers plan to introduce 'Louisa's Law,' a street safety bill in the wake of Boston cyclist's death | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The ghost bike placed in memory of Louisa Gag on Tremont St. in Boston. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR, file)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
It's Friday... the 13th. Time to overcome your fears by brushing up our favorite 23-letter word. (Fingers crossed that you get this Friday morning, as Microsoft Outlook struggles with a global outage.)
Let's get to the news:
Louisa's Law: The family of Louisa Gag is hoping her death can prompt street safety changes — and not just in Boston. The 36-year-old Boston transportation planner was hit and killed by a truck while biking in Mission Hill in July. Now, WBUR's Andrea Perdomo-Hernandez reports that Gag's family is partnering with state lawmakers and safe streets advocates on a multi-pronged bill they plan to introduce in the State House when the next session starts in 2027. "Louisa's Law" combines several previous bills and initiatives that Gag herself was involved with as an advocate.  "These were things that Louisa worked on and cared about," Brendan Kearney, the executive director of WalkMassachusetts, told Andrea. "And she wasn't able to finish this work." Here are the three main components of the bill.
Allow automated cameras for ticketing drivers speeding or running red lights: It's something allowed in 19 states, but not Massachusetts. A bill to change that has repeatedly failed to get through the Legislature since 2020, despite gaining support and other steps in that direction. (Gov. Maura Healey has proposed allowing speed cameras in construction and school zones in her last two budgets, and state lawmakers passed a law last session allowing cameras to fine drivers who don't stop for school buses.) Amid concerns about surveillance and over-policing, supporters note the cameras would only capture the cars' license plates and that the bill would include safeguard to ensure they're implemented equitably.
Close a "loophole" in the state's hands-free driving bill: While Massachusetts has prohibited the use of handheld electronic devices while driving since 2020, there's nothing in the law against streaming video, live broadcasting or taking FaceTime calls while behind the wheel. The bill would close that loophole. A similar proposal was shelved this year, but top members of Healey's administration have signaled support.
Expand truck safety standards: Currently, Massachusetts requires heavy-duty trucks that are owned or directly contracted by state agencies to be outfitted with certain safety devices, including special mirrors and backup cameras. The bill would expand those requirements to trucks owned by city and town governments that operate on public roads.
Mass. questions for Nvida: Rep. Richard Neal is leading an effort by congressional Democrats to investigate President Trump's handling of Nvidia. The leading AI chipmaker's CEO Jensen Huang stepped down yesterday after multiple affairs came to light, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Multiple outlets have reported that Trump was told about the affair back in May (six months before the news broke publicly this week) as the administration granted Nvidia special approval to sell its chips to China. "He chose to do nothing in the name of our national security against our most existential adversary," Rep. Seth Moulton, a fellow Massachusetts Democrat, said on CNN yesterday. "We don't know exactly why, but we've got to find out, and it's time for members of Congress to be asking these tough questions."
Meanwhile: House Republicans are pushing for Huang to testify to Congress in a closed-door meeting on Dec. 1.
The local reaction: The Massachusetts High Technology Council said yesterday that a number of local companies, from Thermo Fisher Scientific to Commonwealth Fusion Systems, rely on Nvidia's chips. "The leadership controversy raises serious questions that deserve scrutiny," Chris Anderson, the council's president, told WBUR in a statement. "But NVIDIA's importance extends well beyond any one executive."
What's a honeytrap? NPR explains the recent history of the spy tactic that appears to have toppled Huang.
Ready or not: Another 2028 ballot question campaign is underway. "The Committee to Restrict Data Centers" announced a campaign yesterday for a ballot question to restrict new data centers in Massachusetts. While not an outright ban, the measure would create strict renewable energy mandates and require a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community, likely discouraging developers from trying in the first place. The campaign plans to begin its signature-gathering efforts next year.
Up in the air: Today's stormy weather across the Northeast is affecting dozens of flights at Logan Airport. As of 7:30 a.m., there are nearly three dozen delays and 29 cancellations, according to FlightAware.
